And it just goes on and on.

And once I'm awake at that hour, that's it. I just cannot get my brain to power down again. I just lay there in the dark, tossing and turning, completely wide awake while the rest of the world is sleeping, thinking about everything I have to do the next day, and it's just... it's driving me absolutely crazy. I just can't keep functioning on this little rest.

Oh, absolutely. I mean, it's not just the nights, the days are honestly just as bad, maybe worse in some ways because I'm actually supposed to be productive. It just feels like every single small delay or tiny hiccup could turn into something major, like this massive catastrophe. If an email takes an hour longer to get a reply to than usual, I'm convinced the deal is dead. It's just exhausting, being on high alert like that all day long, jumping from one worst-case scenario to another. I just can't seem to turn it off, no matter how much I try to just focus on the task in front of me.

Well, wishing I could avoid things? Oh, sure, absolutely. I mean, all the time. Like, internally, I am screaming to just run away from half the things on my calendar. Just looking at my schedule for the week on a Sunday night—which, by the way, I know I shouldn't do, my husband tells me all the time to just close the laptop, but I can't help it—just looking at it makes my chest feel tight. I'll see a one-on-one scheduled with my regional director, and immediately, my brain is just like, "Cancel it. Tell him you're sick. Tell him you have a family emergency." Just this overwhelming urge to escape the situation because I'm already anticipating that he's going to grill me about the Q3 projections, which, honestly, are looking a little soft right now because of supply chain issues that I can't even control, but I know it's going to fall on me. 

So, yes, the *wish* to avoid it is definitely there. I'll sit in my car in the parking garage before work sometimes, just gripping the steering wheel, thinking, "What if I just put it in reverse and drove back home? What if I just got back in bed and pulled the covers over my head?" I play out that entire scenario in my head, just imagining the relief of not having to face the emails, the calls, the constant pressure of everyone needing an answer from me *right now*. It sounds so nice, just for a minute, to disappear from it all. 

But, like I said, I don't actually do it. I never do. I just sit there, feeling sick to my stomach, wishing I could be anywhere else, and then I turn off the car, grab my bag, and walk into the building. Because the anxiety of *not* doing the thing—the guilt, the fear of getting fired, the worry about letting my team down—is somehow even worse than the anxiety of just pushing through it. So I don't avoid it, but boy, do I spend a lot of time wishing I had a magic button to just make it all go away. It's just this constant battle in my head between wanting to hide and feeling like I have to control everything.

Well, changing my routines... I mean, I guess it’s more that it’s changing how I function within those routines. It’s really started affecting both my work and my home life in a big way. Like I was saying about not avoiding things, I still do my job, but the way I do it is just so much harder now. 

Take my pipeline reviews, for example. I used to just go in, look at the numbers, make a call on where we stood, and move on to the next thing. But lately? I spend so much time second-guessing every single decision. I’ll stare at a forecast and think, "Wait, is this rep overly optimistic? Did I miss a red flag in that client email? Should we adjust the projection down by ten percent just to be safe?" And because my brain is doing all of that, the actual review meetings have gotten so incredibly tense. I can feel it in the room. My team is just sitting there, waiting for me to give the green light, and I’m just spinning my wheels, asking them a million tiny follow-up questions that I probably don't even need the answers to, just trying to feel absolutely certain before I commit to a number. It drags everything out and makes everyone, including me, totally miserable.

And then, because I’ve spent eight or ten hours doing *that*—just burning through all this mental energy over-analyzing and worrying and trying to control every little detail—by the time I actually get in my car and drive home, I am just completely depleted. I mean, totally drained. I used to come home, ask my husband about his day, maybe we’d cook dinner together or go for a walk. But now, I walk through the door and I have absolutely nothing left in the tank. 

And I'm so reactive, too. If he asks me a simple question, like "What do you want for dinner?" or "Did you see the mail?", I just snap at him. I don't mean to, but my brain just cannot handle one more decision or one more thing to manage. So instead of spending quality time with him, I just kind of collapse on the couch and zone out. I'm just not fully present with him at all anymore. He'll be talking to me about his day, and I'm just staring at the wall, half-listening, probably worrying about a contract I left on my desk. Which, of course, makes me feel incredibly guilty, because he doesn't deserve that, and then I start worrying that I'm ruining my marriage, which just starts the whole anxiety cycle all over again. So, yeah, I haven't stopped doing my daily activities, but the way I'm functioning during them... it's just really taking a toll on everything.

Should we adjust the projection down by ten percent just to be safe?\" And because my brain is doing all of that, the actual review meetings have gotten so incredibly tense. I can feel it in the room. My team is just sitting there, waiting for me to give the green light, and I’m just spinning my wheels, asking them a million tiny follow-up questions that I probably don't even need the answers to, just trying to feel absolutely certain before I commit to a number. It drags everything out and makes everyone, including me, totally miserable.\n\nAnd then, because I’ve spent eight or ten hours doing *that*—just burning through all this mental energy over-analyzing and worrying and trying to control every little detail—by the time I actually get in my car and drive home, I am just completely depleted. I mean, totally drained. I used to come home, ask my husband about his day, maybe we’d cook dinner together or go for a walk. But now, I walk through the door and I have absolutely nothing left in the tank. \n\nAnd I'm so reactive, too. If he asks me a simple question, like \"What do you want for dinner?\" or \"Did you see the mail?\", I just snap at him. I don't mean to, but my brain just cannot handle one more decision or one more thing to manage. So instead of spending quality time with him, I just kind of collapse on the couch and zone out. I'm just not fully present with him at all anymore. He'll be talking to me about his day, and I'm just staring at the wall, half-listening, probably worrying about a contract I left on my desk. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I mean, when you say specific things, like objects or places... no, not really. It's not like I walk into a specific room and suddenly feel panicked, or like I'm terrified of elevators or dogs or something like that. I actually have a friend who is terrified of bridges, like she will literally drive an hour out of her way to avoid the main highway bridge, but for me, it's nothing like that at all. 

It's more like... it's just a constant hum in the background of everything I do. It doesn't really matter if I'm at the office, or in my car, or sitting on my own couch at home. The anxiety is just there, regardless of my location. It's not triggered by a physical *thing*. It's triggered by my own thoughts, I guess? Like, I could be looking at a completely normal object, like my cell phone, and it's not the phone itself that makes me anxious, it's the spiral of thoughts about who might be emailing me, or what crisis is waiting in my inbox, or if my regional director is trying to get ahold of me about those Q3 numbers I mentioned earlier. 

And it's not specific people, either. I mean, sure, interacting with my boss can be stressful, but I feel just as wound up when I'm talking to my assistant, or my team, or even just sitting entirely alone in my office with the door closed. Or with my husband, like I was saying before. He certainly doesn't make me anxious—he's wonderful, he really is—but I'll be sitting right next to him at the dinner table and my brain is just a million miles away, worrying about a dozen different work scenarios that haven't even happened yet. 

So, yeah, if you're asking if there's a specific trigger, like a certain place I can't go or an object I can't be around... no. I kind of wish it were that simple, honestly. If it was just one thing, like spiders, I could just hire an exterminator or stay away from the woods, you know? But because it's just... life, and my responsibilities, and this constant fear of dropping the ball on literally anything... I can't really escape it by just avoiding a specific place or person. It just comes with me wherever I go.

Well, it's not the interaction itself, if that makes sense. I mean, not because of the actual interacting part. I'm a sales manager, so my entire career is basically built on talking to people. Because if she quits, we're so short-staffed, and training someone new right now would be a disaster. \n\nAnd then it doesn't even stay at work. It bleeds into my personal life, too. I'll suddenly start panicking about the mortgage payment, even though it's on auto-pay and we're fine, but what if something goes wrong with the bank? Or I'll think about a client renewal that isn't even due for three months, but I'm already imagining them walking away. It just feels like every single small delay or tiny hiccup could turn into something major, like this massive catastrophe. If an email takes an hour longer to get a reply to than usual, I'm convinced the deal is dead. It's just exhausting, being on high alert like that all day long, jumping from one worst-case scenario to another. I just can't seem to turn it off, no matter how much I try to just focus on the task in front of me.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or tasks because of your worries or anxiety?\n\nPatient: I don't... I don't really think I avoid things, no. I mean, I still go to all my meetings, I still make all my calls, I still do the performance reviews, even though I might be agonizing over them for days beforehand. It's not like I'm hiding under my desk or calling in sick. Actually, it's almost the opposite? Like, because I'm so worried about everything falling apart, I feel like I have to be involved in *everything*. \n\nLike last week, my assistant was supposed to handle this really straightforward vendor contract, something she's done a million times, but I just couldn't let it go. I kept hovering, asking to see drafts, checking her emails, because I was so terrified she'd miss a clause and we'd be locked into some terrible rate for a year. So I didn't avoid it, I probably over-involved myself. And I do that with my team, too. I'll take on their overflow work instead of just letting them figure it out, because if I do it, at least I know it's done and I don't have to sit there wondering if they're going to drop the ball. \n\nSo, yeah, I'm definitely not avoiding work or situations. I'm just... I'm white-knuckling my way through them, I guess. I'm there, I'm doing the things, but my stomach is in knots the entire time. But I show up. I always show up. I just can't seem to step back and let things happen without feeling like I need to control every single variable to prevent a disaster.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found yourself wishing you could avoid a particular task or situation because of how anxious it makes you feel?\n\nPatient: Well, wishing I could avoid things? Oh, sure, absolutely. I mean, all the time. Like, internally, I am screaming to just run away from half the things on my calendar. Just looking at my schedule for the week on a Sunday night—which, by the way, I know I shouldn't do, my husband tells me all the time to just close the laptop, but I can't help it—just looking at it makes my chest feel tight. I'll see a one-on-one scheduled with my regional director, and immediately, my brain is just like, \"Cancel it. Tell him you're sick. Tell him you have a family emergency.\" Just this overwhelming urge to escape the situation because I'm already anticipating that he's going to grill me about the Q3 projections, which, honestly, are looking a little soft right now because of supply chain issues that I can't even control, but I know it's going to fall on me. \n\nSo, yes, the *wish* to avoid it is definitely there. I'll sit in my car in the parking garage before work sometimes, just gripping the steering wheel, thinking, \"What if I just put it in reverse and drove back home? What if I just got back in bed and pulled the covers over my head?\" I play out that entire scenario in my head, just imagining the relief of not having to face the emails, the calls, the constant pressure of everyone needing an answer from me *right now*. It sounds so nice, just for a minute, to disappear from it all. \n\nBut, like I said, I don't actually do it. I never do. I just sit there, feeling sick to my stomach, wishing I could be anywhere else, and then I turn off the car, grab my bag, and walk into the building. Because the anxiety of *not* doing the thing—the guilt, the fear of getting fired, the worry about letting my team down—is somehow even worse than the anxiety of just pushing through it. So I don't avoid it, but boy, do I spend a lot of time wishing I had a magic button to just make it all go away. It's just this constant battle in my head between wanting to hide and feeling like I have to control everything.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety has caused you to change your daily routines or activities in any way?\n\nPatient: Well, changing my routines... I mean, I guess it’s more that it’s changing how I function within those routines. It’s really started affecting both my work and my home life in a big way. Like I was saying about not avoiding things, I still do my job, but the way I do it is just so much harder now. \n\nTake my pipeline reviews, for example. I used to just go in, look at the numbers, make a call on where we stood, and move on to the next thing. But lately? I spend so much time second-guessing every single decision. I’ll stare at a forecast and think, \"Wait, is this rep overly optimistic? Did I miss a red flag in that client email? Should we adjust the projection down by ten percent just to be safe?\" And because my brain is doing all of that, the actual review meetings have gotten so incredibly tense. I can feel it in the room. My team is just sitting there, waiting for me to give the green light, and I’m just spinning my wheels, asking them a million tiny follow-up questions that I probably don't even need the answers to, just trying to feel absolutely certain before I commit to a number. It drags everything out and makes everyone, including me, totally miserable.\n\nAnd then, because I’ve spent eight or ten hours doing *that*—just burning through all this mental energy over-analyzing and worrying and trying to control every little detail—by the time I actually get in my car and drive home, I am just completely depleted. I mean, totally drained. I used to come home, ask my husband about his day, maybe we’d cook dinner together or go for a walk. But now, I walk through the door and I have absolutely nothing left in the tank. \n\nAnd I'm so reactive, too. If he asks me a simple question, like \"What do you want for dinner?\" or \"Did you see the mail?\", I just snap at him. I don't mean to, but my brain just cannot handle one more decision or one more thing to manage. So instead of spending quality time with him, I just kind of collapse on the couch and zone out. I'm just not fully present with him at all anymore. He'll be talking to me about his day, and I'm just staring at the wall, half-listening, probably worrying about a contract I left on my desk. Which, of course, makes me feel incredibly guilty, because he doesn't deserve that, and then I start worrying that I'm ruining my marriage, which just starts the whole anxiety cycle all over again. So, yeah, I haven't stopped doing my daily activities, but the way I'm functioning during them... it's just really taking a toll on everything.\n\nDoctor: Are there any specific things, like places, objects, or people, that make you feel anxious?\n\nPatient: I mean, when you say specific things, like objects or places... no, not really. It's triggered by my own thoughts, I guess? Like, I could be looking at a completely normal object, like my cell phone, and it's not the phone itself that makes me anxious, it's the spiral of thoughts about who might be emailing me, or what crisis is waiting in my inbox, or if my regional director is trying to get ahold of me about those Q3 numbers I mentioned earlier. \n\nAnd it's not specific people, either. I mean, sure, interacting with my boss can be stressful, but I feel just as wound up when I'm talking to my assistant, or my team, or even just sitting entirely alone in my office with the door closed. Or with my husband, like I was saying before. He certainly doesn't make me anxious—he's wonderful, he really is—but I'll be sitting right next to him at the dinner table and my brain is just a million miles away, worrying about a dozen different work scenarios that haven't even happened yet. \n\nSo, yeah, if you're asking if there's a specific trigger, like a certain place I can't go or an object I can't be around... no. I kind of wish it were that simple, honestly. If it was just one thing, like spiders, I could just hire an exterminator or stay away from the woods, you know? It just comes with me wherever I go.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you're interacting with other people?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not the interaction itself, if that makes sense. You would think so, right? I mean, logically, if you take away the biggest source of stress, the stress itself should go down. I'll be sitting at my desk, and I'll start worrying about whether we're actually going to hit our launch numbers for the new quarter. And then, before I've even figured that out, I'm suddenly stressing about my team. Like, Sarah seemed a little quiet in the morning huddle, is she unhappy? Is she about to quit? Because if she quits, we're so short-staffed, and training someone new right now would be a disaster. \n\nAnd then it doesn't even stay at work. It bleeds into my personal life, too. I'll suddenly start panicking about the mortgage payment, even though it's on auto-pay and we're fine, but what if something goes wrong with the bank? It just feels like every single small delay or tiny hiccup could turn into something major, like this massive catastrophe. It's just exhausting, being on high alert like that all day long, jumping from one worst-case scenario to another. I'll take on their overflow work instead of just letting them figure it out, because if I do it, at least I know it's done and I don't have to sit there wondering if they're going to drop the ball. \n\nSo, yeah, I'm definitely not avoiding work or situations. I'm just... I'm white-knuckling my way through them, I guess. I'm there, I'm doing the things, but my stomach is in knots the entire time. But I show up. I always show up. I just can't seem to step back and let things happen without feeling like I need to control every single variable to prevent a disaster.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found yourself wishing you could avoid a particular task or situation because of how anxious it makes you feel?\n\nPatient: Well, wishing I could avoid things? I just sit there, feeling sick to my stomach, wishing I could be anywhere else, and then I turn off the car, grab my bag, and walk into the building. Because the anxiety of *not* doing the thing—the guilt, the fear of getting fired, the worry about letting my team down—is somehow even worse than the anxiety of just pushing through it. So I don't avoid it, but boy, do I spend a lot of time wishing I had a magic button to just make it all go away. Social interactions? Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't avoid people because I'm anxious about being around them, if that makes sense. It's not like I'm worried they're judging me or that I'm going to say something embarrassing at a party. It's more just... well, like I was saying before, I'm just so incredibly drained by the end of the day.

My first thought is, "I literally do not have the energy to sit there and pretend to be relaxed while my brain is running through a hundred different worst-case scenarios about next quarter's projections." So I guess I do end up saying no to things, or canceling plans, but it's not because the social interaction itself makes me anxious. It's because the anxiety I already have about everything else just completely exhausts me. 

Like last weekend, my friend Sarah—we've known each other since college—she had this little get-together for her birthday. Nothing crazy, just a few people at her place. And I really wanted to go! I had bought her a gift and everything. But Friday night, after a whole week of stressing over pipeline reports and worrying about whether my top rep was going to jump ship to a competitor, I just... I couldn't do it. I texted her Saturday morning and said I had a migraine. Which, honestly, wasn't entirely a lie, because my head was pounding from all the tension. But the real reason was just that I knew if I went, I wouldn't be able to turn my brain off. I'd be sitting there with a glass of wine, nodding along to whatever story someone was telling, but internally I'd be obsessing over whether I forgot to CC the VP on an email, or if that slight delay in a client's response meant they were pulling out of the deal. It's just not fair to them, and it's exhausting for me. So, no, I don't avoid socializing because I'm scared of socializing. I just avoid it because I don't have any bandwidth left for it.

He certainly doesn't make me anxious—he's wonderful, he really is—but I'll be sitting right next to him at the dinner table and my brain is just a million miles away, worrying about a dozen different work scenarios that haven't even happened yet. \n\nSo, yeah, if you're asking if there's a specific trigger, like a certain place I can't go or an object I can't be around... no. I kind of wish it were that simple, honestly. If it was just one thing, like spiders, I could just hire an exterminator or stay away from the woods, you know? But because it's just... life, and my responsibilities, and this constant fear of dropping the ball on literally anything... I can't really escape it by just avoiding a specific place or person. It just comes with me wherever I go.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you're interacting with other people?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not the interaction itself, if that makes sense. I mean, not because of the actual interacting part. I'm a sales manager, so my entire career is basically built on talking to people. If I were afraid of talking to people, I would definitely be in the wrong profession! I'm on calls with clients all day, I'm doing one-on-ones with my reps, I'm presenting to the regional directors... I can talk to a brick wall. So it's not like I get butterflies because I have to say hello to someone or because I'm worried about making small talk at a networking event. It's not that kind of social panic where I'm worried people are judging me or anything like that. \n\nBut... am I anxious *while* I'm interacting with them? Yes, absolutely, but that's really just because I'm anxious all the time anyway, like I was saying before. It's the background noise. Like, I could be sitting across from one of my best account executives—someone I've known for five years, totally comfortable with him as a person, we joke around all the time—and I'm still sitting there with my stomach completely tied in knots. But I'm not anxious about *him*. I'm anxious about the fact that his territory is underperforming this quarter, and while he's talking to me about his weekend, I'm running through fourteen different scenarios in my head about how I'm going to explain his numbers to my boss on Friday. \n\nSo I'm nodding, and I'm smiling, and I'm saying all the right things in the conversation, but internally I'm just vibrating with stress about the actual work. It's not the socializing. It's just that my brain never shuts off the worrying, no matter who happens to be standing in front of me. I could be chatting with the barista at the coffee shop about the weather, and I'd still be stressing about my pipeline forecast, you know?\n\nDoctor: Have you started to avoid certain tasks or situations because they might trigger or worsen your anxiety?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, I kind of touched on this a little bit earlier, but I really don't avoid things. It’s almost like... I don't even have the luxury of avoiding anything, you know? If I started putting off tasks at work just because they made me stressed, my entire department would completely fall apart. I have a team of reps relying on me, I have regional directors breathing down my neck for those Q3 numbers, so I can't just hide under my desk, as much as I might want to sometimes. \n\nSo, no, I don't avoid the situations. I still open every single email, I still run every single pipeline review, I still have all the hard conversations. It's actually almost the exact opposite of avoiding them, if that makes sense? Like, I’ll sit at my computer and agonize over a simple forecast spreadsheet for two hours when it should take twenty minutes, just double and triple-checking everything because I'm so worried about getting it wrong or missing something crucial. \n\nIt would probably be a relief to just avoid it and say, \"Oh, I'll deal with this tomorrow,\" but my brain just won't let me do that either. The worry about *not* doing the task is just as bad as the worry *during* the task. I mean, logically, if you take away the biggest source of stress, the stress itself should go down. So, yeah, it's definitely not just focused on work. It just bleeds into literally every single part of my life, all day long.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your anxiety is interfering with your ability to enjoy or participate in activities that you normally like to do?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, absolutely. It just comes with me wherever I go.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you're interacting with other people?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not the interaction itself, if that makes sense. I mean, I kind of touched on this a little bit earlier, but I really don't avoid things. It’s almost like... I don't even have the luxury of avoiding anything, you know? If I started putting off tasks at work just because they made me stressed, my entire department would completely fall apart. I have a team of reps relying on me, I have regional directors breathing down my neck for those Q3 numbers, so I can't just hide under my desk, as much as I might want to sometimes. \n\nSo, no, I don't avoid the situations. Well, I think... honestly, I feel like I've kind of already touched on this a bit, right? I mean, when we were talking earlier about how I view myself, it's pretty much the same thing. My self-confidence itself hasn't really taken a hit, not at its core. Like, I still know I'm good at my job. I know I didn't get to be a sales manager at 32 by accident, you know? I worked incredibly hard for my degree, I grinded through the lower-level positions, I proved myself quarter after quarter. So that foundational belief in my abilities, that hasn't disappeared just because I'm dealing with all this... noise in my head.

But, I guess, if I'm really thinking about it... it's more that the anxiety just makes it so exhausting to access that confidence sometimes. Like, the confidence is there, sitting in a box, but the anxiety has stacked a hundred heavy boxes of "what-ifs" on top of it. So when I'm staring at a forecasting spreadsheet, my brain isn't saying, "You don't know how to do this." It's saying, "What if you missed one tiny variable that throws off the entire projection and ruins the quarter for the whole team?" 

So the self-doubt isn't about my overall competence, it's about the execution in that exact moment. It's like I have to fight through this thick fog of panic just to remind myself that I actually do know what I'm doing. And that's what's so frustrating! I'll be sitting in a meeting, feeling my heart racing, sweating, absolutely convinced I'm about to say the wrong thing and derail a major account, but at the exact same time, there's this logical part of my brain going, "You literally closed three deals exactly like this last year, you know the strategy." 

So, no, I wouldn't say my actual self-confidence has changed or diminished. I don't feel like a lesser person or a failure. It's just... overshadowed, I guess? It's just so much harder to hold onto it when every single minor decision feels like it has life-or-death stakes attached to it. But the confidence itself? Yeah, like I said before, that's still intact. I just wish it didn't feel like such a battle to actually use it every day.
